hook.line: Seat your queen on the central throne and ring her with six guards to win. The oldest known board game played on hexagonal cells.
hook.say: Let me show you the story of Agon.

p: Agon was published in London in 1842 as “Agon, or the Queen's Guards; a new game of skill”. It is credited to Anthony Peacock, and the rules appeared under the name of Thomas Sherwin.
It is the oldest known board game played on hexagonal cells. Victorian makers such as Jaques & Son sold handsome boards and pieces.

ch.say: A one-way road — never back out!
ch.cap: 91 cells; each queen and six guards alternate round the edge
p: A piece steps along its ring or one ring inwards — never outwards.
Sandwich an enemy piece in a line to capture it. It stays on the board, and its owner must relocate it on the next turn: a guard to the edge, the queen to any empty cell.

ch.say: Hexagonal cells spread to many games later on.
